paragraphs.source_en: On the night of the eighth day of the sixth month of Tenshō 10, Hashiba Chikuzen-no-kami Hideyoshi withdrew his troops from Takamatsu, passed through Numa Castle in Bizen, and entered his own seat at Himeji. By then, Nagahama in Ōmi had fallen to Mitsuhide, and Hideyoshi's mother had fled to Himeji Castle for refuge.

units.source_en: On the night of the eighth day of the sixth month of Tenshō 10, Hashiba Chikuzen-no-kami Hideyoshi withdrew his troops from Takamatsu, passed through Numa Castle in Bizen, and entered his own seat at Himeji.

paragraphs.source_zh: 天正十年六月初八夜，羽柴筑前守秀吉从高松撤兵，途经备前的沼城，驻进了自己的居城姬路。此时，近江的长滨已被光秀攻陷，秀吉的母亲逃到姬路城来避难。

paragraphs.source_en: “It is already midnight. I shall see Mother tomorrow.” With that, Hideyoshi hurriedly took Koide Harima and Miyoshi Musashi, who had remained to guard the castle, on a tour of its defenses; he meant to verify every report for himself.

units.source_en: “It is already midnight. I shall see Mother tomorrow.”
units.source_zh: “已经半夜了，明天再见母亲吧。”

paragraphs.source_en: Since the crisis had erupted without warning, not every report was necessarily favorable to Hideyoshi. In Kyoto, Mitsuhide sought popular favor by bestowing a generous gift upon the people—the remission of ground rent. He then invaded Ōmi. His army met almost no resistance. Only the brothers of Yamaoka Mimasaka-no-kami burned the great bridge at Seta, delaying Mitsuhide's advance a little; everything thereafter proceeded smoothly, just as anticipated.

paragraphs.source_en: The key to victory or defeat lay in where the loyalties of the daimyō around the Kinai region would fall. Among them were Mitsuhide's former retainers Takayama Ukon and Nakagawa Kiyohide, both also related to him, as well as his sworn friends Hosokawa Fujitaka and his son, and Tsutsui Junkei. Only one man seemed highly likely to become Hideyoshi's ally: Ikeda Nobuteru of Hanakuma in Settsu, whose childhood name was Katsusaburō and who, like Hideyoshi, had long served under Nobunaga.
